title: Permanent vs. temporary employees: when to hire each.
summary: Learn when to hire permanent vs. temporary employees, how to balance both models, and how to build a workforce mix that fits your business roadmap.
body_markdown:
### Key takeaways:


- Permanent hires fit ongoing work that depends on institutional knowledge, a long ramp-up, or a pipeline of future leaders.
- Temporary and contract staffing fits work with a defined endpoint, an urgent start date, a new function to test, or an employee on extended leave.
- Permanent headcount is largely a fixed cost and temporary staffing is a variable one. The balance between them determines how easily the business can adjust to demand.
- A temporary need that keeps coming back is a signal to look at the cause, and sometimes to convert the role.
- The strongest workforce strategies pair a stable permanent core with a flexible layer of temporary talent and revisit the mix as plans change.


When a manager is waiting and a deadline is close, employers often choose between a permanent and a temporary hire based only on the role that needs filling right now. Each call can make sense in the moment, but it's easy to lose sight of how those individual decisions add up across the workforce. Some teams end up with permanent headcount they can't keep busy in a slow quarter, while others keep cycling temporary workers through jobs the business now needs year-round.


A stronger approach treats the permanent and temporary mix as a planning decision tied to where the business is headed. This guide covers how each model works and what it costs, when each one makes the most sense, and how to build a mix that can adjust as plans change.


## How permanent vs. temporary employee models work


Most staffing decisions come down to two engagement models, each of which puts a different set of costs and commitments on the employer.


**Permanent employees** join your payroll with no set end date. They're typically eligible for benefits and can grow into new roles over time, which makes them a natural fit for work the business runs every day.


**Temporary employees** work for a fixed period or until a project wraps. When they come through a staffing partner, that firm usually acts as the employer of record and takes on payroll, taxes, and benefits administration, which is the core of


[how staffing agencies work](https://www.kellyservices.com/insights/how-do-staffing-agencies-work) .


Contract-to-hire


is a variation that starts as a temporary assignment with the intent to convert, giving both sides time to judge fit before a permanent offer.


A permanent employee is largely a fixed cost, since salary and benefits continue whether the workload is heavy or light, and


[benefits accounted for 31.5% of employer compensation costs](https://www.bls.gov/opub/ted/2026/compensation-costs-for-private-industry-workers-averaged-46-89-per-hour-worked-in-june-2026.htm) for full-time private industry workers in June 2026. Temporary and contract workers are a variable cost. The employer pays the staffing partner an hourly bill rate that covers the worker's pay along with the payroll and benefits costs the partner carries, and spending stops when the assignment ends. Most workforces need some of each, and the balance between fixed and flexible costs gives employers room to adjust when demand changes.


## When permanent hires are most strategic


Permanent hiring is an investment in continuity, institutional knowledge, and the people who will lead the business later. It pays off most in three situations.


1. **The work is ongoing and core to the business.** Roles at the center of daily operations become more valuable the longer someone holds them. A quality engineer in a regulated plant, a lab manager who knows the history behind every validated process, and a controller who closes the books each month all rely on knowing how the organization works. Functions that carry significant risk, such as information security, also benefit from people who stay.


2. **You're building a leadership pipeline.**


[Promoting from within](https://www.kellyservices.com/insights/what-is-internal-mobility) depends on people who have had time to learn the organization. Employees who move up already know the customers, systems, and unwritten rules, so they start new roles with context an outside hire has to build from scratch.


3. **Retention is part of the return.** Benefits and career development are easier to justify when ramp-up is long and knowledge is hard to replace, because every departure restarts the cycle of recruiting, onboarding, and ramp-up. When a permanent seat does open,


[direct sourcing and hiring](https://www.kellyservices.com/workforce-solutions/direct-sourcing-hiring/) can shorten the search.


## When temporary or contract staffing is the better fit


Temporary and contract staffing works best when the business needs specific skills or extra capacity for a defined period. Four situations favor this model.


1. **The work has a defined endpoint.** Peak season at a distribution center, a clinical study with a fixed enrollment window, a plant expansion, and a year-end close all have a finish line. Staffing them with temporary talent lets the business scale back when the work wraps, without layoffs or idle headcount.


2. **You need people in place quickly.** Contract roles often clear budget approval much faster than a permanent headcount request, which can take months to move through finance. Contract-to-hire works as a bridge here, since a contractor can start now and convert once the permanent role is approved.


3. **You're testing a new function.** A contract engagement lets the business confirm a new capability is needed, and learn what the role requires, before committing to permanent headcount. If the need holds, the employer can convert the role with a sharper job description and a candidate who has already proven a good fit.


4. **Someone is out for an extended period.** Parental leave, medical leave, and other long absences leave work that still has to get done. Employees returning from


[FMLA leave are generally entitled to the same or an equivalent job](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/fmla/employer-guide) , so temporary coverage keeps the work moving without adding a hire the team won't need afterward.


Temporary talent contributes the most when managers onboard contractors the way they would a new employee, with clear expectations and regular feedback. That approach is central to


[treating temporary talent as a strategic resource](https://www.kellyservices.com/insights/temporary-staffing-business-flexibility) .


Co-employment is a normal part of working with a staffing partner, and an experienced partner helps manage it. Long assignments still deserve a periodic check. When a temporary worker stays in the same role for years and is managed like any other employee, it's worth reviewing how the arrangement is structured. If the need has become permanent, converting the role is usually the cleaner path.


## How to decide for a specific role


Placing a role in the mix comes down to five steps, each focused on the work itself, and the answers usually point clearly toward one model.


1. **Gauge how steady demand is.** Work that runs at the same level all year supports permanent headcount. Work that rises and falls with seasons, contracts, or order volume is a natural fit for temporary talent.


2. **Assess institutional knowledge** If a departure would take customer relationships, proprietary processes, or regulatory history out the door, the role belongs with permanent staff.


3. **Weigh ramp-up time.** The longer it takes someone to become productive, the more each departure costs, which strengthens the case for a permanent hire.


4. **Check which budget is available.** Project funding is often available sooner than approved headcount, so a contract or contract-to-hire role can get work started while a permanent request moves through approval.


5. **Look at whether the need keeps coming back.** When the same temporary role gets filled again and again, ask why. Steady growth may mean the role has become permanent and is ready to convert. Repeated turnover, a scheduling policy, or a management issue points to a problem that neither model will fix on its own.


These steps settle the call for one role. Applied across the whole workforce, they show what the overall mix should look like.


## Why the strongest workforce strategies use both


Most organizations do best with a stable permanent core and a flexible layer of temporary and contract talent around it. The busier the peaks and the quieter the slow periods, the larger that flexible layer should be.


### A flexible layer protects and feeds the permanent core


Permanent employees hold the relationships, leadership, and


[institutional knowledge the business can't afford to lose](https://www.kellyservices.com/insights/how-to-preserve-institutional-knowledge-before-it-walks-out-the-door) . Temporary and contract talent covers seasonal peaks, project work, and skills the business needs for a limited stretch. Demand for that flexible layer follows a familiar yearly rhythm, with


[staffing employment usually lowest early in the year and climbing to a fourth-quarter peak](https://americanstaffing.net/posts/2026/06/25/seasonal-declines-narrow-in-first-quarter-of-2026/) . A flexible layer lets the business follow its own version of that curve without hiring ahead of demand or cutting core staff when volume drops.


The flexible layer can also feed the core. Temporary workers who prove themselves on the job can move into permanent roles, and the employer makes those offers with far more to go on than an interview. A precision care technology company that works with Kelly saw this firsthand. It capped tenure for its part-time field workers and kept losing trained people, along with the process knowledge they carried. Through a


[Business Process Outsourcing program](https://www.kellyservices.com/insights/bpo-case-study-retaining-proprietary-intel-and-top-talent) , Kelly employed those workers directly, which gave managers time to see who thrived before making full-time offers. Over four years, 28 top performers joined the company as full-time employees.


### A planned mix can adjust as the business changes


The mix holds up best when it's set as part of a multiyear plan that accounts for every type of worker, including permanent, temporary, contract, independent, and outsourced talent, at every level of the organization. The first step in any


[workforce planning process](https://www.kellyservices.com/insights/workforce-planning-guide) is a clear count of who does the work today.


Once the plan exists, the mix of permanent and temporary talent needs regular review. A product launch, new technology, a change in the market, or a temporary need that keeps coming back are all signs the current blend may no longer fit.


Kelly supports every part of that mix, from temporary staffing and direct hire to


[business process outsourcing](https://www.kellyservices.com/workforce-solutions/business-process-outsourcing/) . If your current blend no longer matches where the business is headed,


[talk with a Kelly workforce expert](https://www.kellyservices.com/workforce-solutions/) about building one that does.
